docs.whatis.title: What is UnityGameTranslator?
docs.whatis.pitch: UnityGameTranslator is a mod you drop into a Unity game to play it in your language. The game doesn't need to offer that language, and its developer doesn't need to lift a finger: the mod picks up the text as the game displays it, and translates it.
docs.whatis.mod_desc: Runs inside the game and translates as you play: a community translation when one exists, your AI for the rest — local (free, offline) or online with your own key.
docs.whatis.site_desc: The community library: find a translation for your game, publish yours, and improve them together with the web editors and the quality system.
docs.whatis.flow_step1: The mod detects which game you're playing.
docs.whatis.flow_step2: In online mode, it looks for a community translation of that game and offers to download it.
docs.whatis.flow_step3: Lines nobody has translated yet are translated live by your AI — locally on your machine, or online if you plugged in your key.
docs.whatis.flow_step4: Everything lives in a single local file on your machine — the game stays translated even offline.
docs.whatis.flow_step5: Share that file if you feel like it: the community validates, fixes and improves it over time.
docs.whatis.privacy_desc: Your AI key, your settings and your translation file stay on your machine. Nothing goes public until you explicitly publish it, and you only need an account to share.
docs.whatis.dev_desc: UnityGameTranslator is not a localization SDK. We are exploring one, though — a way for a game to plug into community translations directly and let players translate it.
docs.whatis.dev_cta: Interested? Come talk to us in the GitHub Discussions.

docs.editing.title: Editing your translation
docs.editing.intro: Two editors let you polish your translation without stopping the game: a quick text editor right inside it, and a full browser editor synced live with your session.
docs.editing.text_editor_intro: Fix a translation the moment you spot it, without leaving the game.
docs.editing.text_editor_step1: Open the mod panel (Ctrl+F10) → Translation Tools, and click Start Text Editor in the Tools tab.
docs.editing.text_editor_step2: Click any translated text in the game to open it in the editor.
docs.editing.text_editor_step3: Edit the translation and save — it is applied on screen immediately and marked Human (H). You can also send the line back to the AI with Retranslate.
docs.editing.text_editor_alt: The in-game Element Inspector with a selected element and its editable texts
docs.editing.text_editor_caption: Pick an element on screen: every text it contains can be edited or re-translated
docs.editing.placeholders_desc: Numbers that change while playing (damage, gold, timers) appear as [!v*0], [!v*1]… placeholders. Keep them in your text: the mod re-injects the live values, and the editor warns you if your edit breaks them.
docs.editing.text_editor_limits_desc: While you type, the game still catches keyboard input (this cannot be prevented), which can make longer edits awkward. The in-game editor shines at picking a text directly on screen — for real editing sessions, prefer the browser editor and its full toolset.
docs.editing.live_edit_intro: Reworking hundreds of lines calls for a real keyboard and a big screen. The browser editor opens your LOCAL translation file in a web page — no account, nothing published — and stays in sync with the game, both ways.
docs.editing.mod_tools_alt: The Tools tab of the mod with the Text Editor and Browser Editor sections
docs.editing.mod_tools_caption: The mod's Tools tab: the entry point of both in-game editors
docs.editing.session_active_alt: The Tools tab while a browser session is active
docs.editing.session_active_caption: While the session is active, each browser save is applied in-game
docs.editing.live_edit_step1: In the mod: Translation Tools → Edit in browser. Your browser opens the editor on your local file.
docs.editing.live_edit_step2: Edit, validate or delete lines, then click Save & apply in game: the changes are hot-reloaded in-game within seconds.
docs.editing.live_edit_step3: Keep playing: new AI translations appear in the editor as you play (the 'New from the game' filter collects them for review).
docs.editing.live_edit_alt: The browser live edit page with search, filters, quality bar and the translation table
docs.editing.live_edit_caption: The live editor: quality bar, filters, search & replace, and per-line actions
docs.editing.retranslate_desc: If an AI backend is configured in the mod, a wand button appears on each line. The website only CALLS your mod: the request travels over the session channel, your mod translates with the local configuration YOU set up (your backend, your model, your key), and only the translated text comes back. No API key or LLM configuration is ever exchanged or stored on the website — everything personal stays on your machine.
docs.editing.lifecycle_desc: A session only ends when you close the browser page or quit the game — never on a timer. Play for hours and come back to edit whenever you want. When the session ends, its temporary file is deleted from the server.
docs.editing.web_edit_intro: Translations you shared on the website have their own editor too — same interface, same tools.
docs.editing.web_edit_step1: Open My Translations, pick a translation and click Edit.
docs.editing.web_edit_step2: Edit, validate or delete lines exactly like in the live editor, then save.
docs.editing.web_edit_step3: The mod detects the update at the next game launch and offers to download or merge it.
docs.editing.toolbox_intro: The same tools are available in every web editor (live edit, merge view and compare view):
docs.editing.toolbox_search: Search with highlighting, match counter and Enter / Shift+Enter navigation — the search survives page refreshes.
docs.editing.toolbox_replace: Replace, one line at a time: you see each line before changing it, so replacements are marked Human (H).
docs.editing.toolbox_keyboard: Keyboard review: ↑↓ move the row cursor, V validates, E edits, Del deletes.
docs.editing.toolbox_validate: One click on an AI-tagged line validates it (A → V); devalidating is always an explicit tag action.
docs.editing.toolbox_quality: The quality bar shows the human-reviewed share of the file (H+V) and moves as you work.
docs.editing.toolbox_placeholders: A placeholder guard warns when an edit would break [!v*N] dynamic values.

docs.quality_system.title: Translation tags
docs.quality_system.intro: Every line of a translation carries a tag saying where its final wording came from. The coloured bar shown on each translation is built from them.
docs.quality_system.validated_desc: Machine wording a human read and accepted
docs.quality_system.ai_desc: Machine wording nobody has read yet
docs.quality_system.skip_desc: A human ruled that this line stays as it is: a fictional language, a proper name, text that must not change

docs.algorithms.title: How the numbers work
docs.algorithms.intro: Every figure this site shows about a translation comes from a formula, and all of them are published below. They exist to help you pick a translation and to let an author see where their work stands.
docs.algorithms.stage_desc: The share of a file whose wording a human settled: written, accepted, or deliberately kept. Shown as a step rather than a mark, because every translation begins as machine output — that is a starting point, not a failing grade. A file with nothing translated has no stage at all.
docs.algorithms.rate_desc: The same share, weighted by the evidence behind the accepted lines. Accepting the machine's wording is review, and on a short game it may well be right everywhere — nobody should have to retype correct text. But approving a whole file without reading it leaves exactly the same tags as reading it carefully. Accepted lines therefore count in full as soon as one line in ten was written or kept by hand, and never count for less than 0.8.
docs.algorithms.rate_limit: This separates the careless from the careful. It does not stop someone determined to inflate their figures, which is a matter for moderation rather than for arithmetic.
docs.algorithms.coverage_desc: How much of the game a translation actually reaches. The true amount of text in a game cannot be known — it is captured as players meet it — but the other translations of the same game measure it: the same lines turn up as people get further, whatever language they translate into. The largest of them sets the yardstick.
docs.algorithms.coverage_caveat: It is a lower bound, never the real size, and it rises as people play further. When a game has a single published translation, that one is the yardstick.
docs.algorithms.order_desc: Which translation is offered first. Coverage sets the ceiling and review lifts within it, so a complete machine translation still comes before a flawless fragment. Votes and downloads are added, and a bonus goes to a fork keeping abandoned work alive. Work still in progress fades as it stands still; a translation its author has declared finished keeps its rank, and loses it when another translation of the same game goes further.
docs.algorithms.order_base: The 0.5 is an editorial choice rather than a technical one: it is what merely existing is worth against having been reviewed. Someone about to play a whole game needs the text to be there first.
docs.algorithms.visibility_desc: The composition bar, the review stage and the game coverage are shown to everyone. The review rate is shown to a translation's author, on their own pages. The ordering score is never displayed: it only decides the order.
docs.quality_system.capture_desc: In capture mode the mod records the original text as it appears on screen, without translating it. Ideal for building a 100% human translation from scratch. Captured text carries tag 'H' with an empty value, waiting for someone to write it.

legal.intellectual_property_text: The UnityGameTranslator mod is open source and available under its respective license on GitHub. User-submitted translations remain the property of their authors. Game names and images belong to their respective owners.
legal.privacy_intro: This privacy policy explains how we collect, use, and protect your personal data when you use UnityGameTranslator.
legal.who_responsible: This site is run by an individual. The name, address and hosting provider are given in the
legal.who_complaints: If you think your data is mishandled, tell us — and if that does not settle it, you can lodge a complaint with the CNIL, the French data protection authority. Write to us at
legal.what_we_hold: What we hold, and how it reached us
legal.hold_account_local: If you sign up here, we store the username you chose and your password, which is hashed and which nobody can read back, including us. Recovery codes are stored the same way. No email address is asked for and none is stored.
legal.hold_account_platform: If you sign in with another platform — Steam, Google, GitHub, Discord or Twitch — we store the identifier that platform gives us, the display name it returns, and your email address when it provides one. Steam does not provide one, so we generate an address that receives nothing and goes nowhere. We never receive your password on any of them.
legal.hold_account_public: Your display name is public. Your email address never is.
legal.hold_published_text: The translations you upload, the votes you cast and the reports you send. They stay attached to your account for as long as it exists — and after it, see "Your Rights" below.
legal.hold_connections_why: Every sign-in, every upload and every access token we issue is recorded with your IP address and your browser's identification. We are required to keep this: French law asks anyone hosting content published by others to be able to identify who contributed it.
legal.hold_connections_end: The IP address is erased after twelve months, automatically. The record of the act stays, no longer attached to an address.
legal.hold_accesses_text: When you link a game or the Manager to your account, we record which program asked, the name you gave the device, and — when the program says — which game. The game's name is kept encrypted, and nothing here identifies your machine. You can see the whole list, and cut any of it, under Linked devices in your profile.
legal.hold_counting_no_cookie: We count page views to know which games interest people. No cookie is used for this.
legal.hold_counting_how: Each visit is reduced to a fingerprint computed from your IP address, your browser's identification and the current date. It cannot be reversed into any of them. The country is guessed from your browser's language setting, never from your IP address, and we use no geolocation service.
legal.hold_counting_forgotten: The fingerprint is erased the following night, as soon as the day's total has been worked out, and the key that produced it is destroyed with it. From then on nobody — ourselves included — can check whether a given address visited: the answer is kept, the working-out is gone.
legal.hold_counting_retention: The visits themselves are erased after 90 days. Only totals — how many views, how many downloads — are kept beyond that, and they name nobody.
legal.hold_programs: What the mod and the Manager send
legal.hold_programs_mod: The mod, inside your game, asks our site whether a translation exists for that game, downloads the one you choose, and sends back what you publish. When you link it to your account it also names the game, so that access is one you can recognise later. It checks for updates to itself.
legal.hold_programs_manager: The Manager finds Unity games on your machine — in the folders used by Steam, Epic and GOG, and in folders you add. It does not search your disks. If you allow it, it asks our site whether translations exist for the games it found, sending their names or Steam identifiers, and checks which mod loaders and versions have been published. It asks before doing any of this, and it works offline if you say no.
legal.hold_programs_never: Neither ever sends the contents of your games.
legal.keep_content_for: Until you erase them, or your account
legal.keep_accesses_for: Until you revoke them, and at most one year
legal.keep_notifications_for: 12 months, or until you delete them
legal.keep_ip: IP address in the connection record
legal.keep_session_for: Until you close your browser (7 days at most)
legal.keep_remember_for: 30 days, and only if you tick it
legal.sharing_none: We sell nothing and share nothing for anybody else's purposes.
legal.sharing_but: Some things nonetheless leave this machine, and you should know which:
legal.sharing_host: Our host keeps the site's backups. It is a French company and the data stays in France. A limited number of restore points is kept, and the oldest fall away as new ones arrive.
legal.sharing_platform: The platform you sign in with knows you signed in — that is what signing in is.
legal.sharing_images: Game cover images are loaded from Steam, IGDB and RAWG. Your browser fetches them directly, so those services see your IP address. So does the platform hosting an avatar, when you use one.
legal.sharing_github: GitHub is contacted by the mod and by the Manager to fetch mod loaders and check versions, which shows them your IP address.
legal.sharing_caveat: We cannot say your data never leaves Europe, because the four above are not all in Europe. What we can say is that we send nothing to any of them on purpose.
legal.cookie_remember: Set only if you ask to stay signed in, and then for thirty days. Signing out removes it.
legal.right_see: See everything we hold about you — Profile, then Export my data. It includes your account, your translations, your votes, your reports and the connection record with its IP addresses.
legal.right_correct: Correct your display name — Profile. Once every 30 days.
legal.right_erase: Erase your account — Profile, then Delete account. Your name, address, password and every way of signing in are erased immediately and irreversibly. Your published translations stay by default, credited to a deleted account nobody can trace back to you; a box lets you remove them instead, and the screen lists what would go.
legal.right_object: Object, or ask us to restrict what we do — write to us.
legal.right_take: Take your data elsewhere — the export above is a JSON file.
legal.right_complain: Complain to the CNIL — see "Who we are" above.
legal.rights_limit: Erasure has one limit, and it is not ours. The connection record above is kept for twelve months even after an account is erased, because the law requires it; it no longer carries your name. And a backup restored from before your request could bring back what you erased — we keep a list of erasures so they can be applied again, but if the live database were lost entirely that list would go with it.

docs.algorithms.completeness_desc: How much of what a translation has already met in game is translated. The mod records every text it runs into, so lines nobody has translated yet are known and counted — unlike the rest of the game, whose size nobody knows. This is the only measure here that needs no other translation to compare against.
docs.algorithms.completeness_floor: Silent when nothing is pending. Below 90%, the review stage is not shown at all: reviewing and translating are two different jobs, and judging how well a text was read before it is written says nothing.

seo.home_description: Open-source mod that translates Unity games while you play: community translations, hand-written ones, free local AI, or an online service with your own key.
docs.quick_start.discovery: There is no one-click extraction of a whole game. The mod reads the text Unity actually displays, so a line becomes known the moment it first shows up on screen — and a game reveals its text as you play through it. That is also why a translation is never "finished": it grows as people get further.
docs.config.gui_intro: None of this needs the configuration file. Everything lives in the Translation tab of the options panel, opened in game with the settings hotkey. The Type menu decides where translations come from, and Manual Mode at the top collects the game's texts without translating them, so you can write them yourself afterwards.
docs.config.gui_ai_alt: Translation tab, Type set to AI (local or cloud)
docs.config.gui_ai_caption: A local or cloud AI: the address of your server, a key if it asks for one, and the model. Ollama or LM Studio on your own machine usually needs no key.
docs.config.gui_tools_alt: Translation tab, Type set to Google / DeepL
docs.config.gui_tools_caption: An online service: pick the provider and paste your own key. They bill you directly — the mod talks to them from your machine, never through this site.
docs.algorithms.dormancy_desc: Finished and abandoned look alike from outside: in both cases nothing moves. What tells them apart is the rhythm of the person behind the file. So the silence a translation is allowed is the span it was actually worked on - from when it was first published to its last change - between two weeks and three months. Somebody who kept a translation up for seven months and has been quiet for six weeks is on holiday; one worked on for ten days and silent since is over, because most games are played once and the only engine moving a translation forward is somebody playing.
docs.algorithms.dormancy_note: Used to tell a contributor that the translation they are helping has gone quiet, and to credit a fork that picked up an abandoned one. A finished translation is never dormant by the clock - it will not change again, and that is the point of finishing; what can push it aside is a rival covering more of the game, never the calendar. A translation holding no translated line at all counts as dormant whatever its dates say.
docs.config.never_share: Your keys are stored encrypted and tied to your machine, so a copy taken elsewhere cannot be read. That protects the copy, not the machine: on your own computer the protection is obfuscation, not a wall. The file also holds your site token. Your keys never leave your machine — the mod talks to each provider directly.
docs.config.table_intro: The settings panel covers everyday use. What follows is what only the file reaches — and what can bite.
docs.config.update_frequency: How often the site is asked whether something changed: auto, never, startup, 30m, 1h, realtime. Auto lets the mod choose from your role — an open connection for an author, a check at startup for a player. Replaces the old check_update_on_start, which is now read once to migrate and then dropped.
docs.config.notify_prereleases: Also hear about beta releases. Off by default: most people should only be told about stable ones.
docs.config.ignored_uuids: Translation lineages this install stops offering to update. Filled by the mod when you dismiss an update for good.
docs.config.detection_latency: How long a text may sit on screen before the mod notices it. Lower reacts faster and costs more CPU; the scan is spread across frames, so even low values stay under the natural frame-time noise.
docs.config.timeout: Milliseconds before a translation request is given up on. Raise it for a slow local model on a modest machine.
docs.config.rate_limit: Seconds to wait before retrying when the service answers "too many requests". Applies to every backend, decimals allowed.
docs.config.atlas_size: Resolution ceiling for a rasterized replacement font. 0 means 4096; raising it to 8192 gives crisper text when scaled up, at a video-memory cost. Layout-neutral, so it is safe on an already published translation.
docs.config.api_base_url: Point the mod at another server. null uses the address it was built with. website_base_url and sse_base_url work the same way — for running your own instance.
docs.config.token_server: Which server issued the token in this file. Written by the mod, not by you: if the address changes, the token is dropped rather than replayed against someone else's server.
docs.config.proxy_mode: default follows whatever the game set, system asks the operating system afresh, none goes straight out, custom uses proxy_url. Try none when a connection test hangs on "Testing…".
docs.config.proxy_url: Address of your own proxy, used when proxy_mode is custom. proxy_username and proxy_password go with it; proxy_bypass_local keeps local addresses direct.
docs.config.localization_fallback: Last resort when some text escapes every other method: translates at the string level. It ignores the per-element font settings, so only turn it on if text is genuinely being missed.
docs.config.strict_source: Experimental, and off for a reason: asks the model to skip anything that is not in the source language. It can silently drop text that was fine.
docs.config.translate_mod_ui: Whether the mod's own interface is translated. Absent means the translation decides — a file carrying mod-UI lines was written with a translated interface. true or false overrides it here.

auth.register_privacy: An account records only what the law requires, and it is only needed to share translations. What that covers, and for how long, is set out in the

auth.codes_hint: Save them in a password manager, or print them.
auth.recover_intro: Use one of your recovery codes to set a new password. The code is consumed.
auth.recover_note: Recovery codes only exist for local accounts. If you signed in with Steam, Discord, Google... just use that platform's button.
auth.recovered: Welcome back! Your password has been updated — consider regenerating your recovery codes from your profile.

docs.quick_start.way_manager_desc: A program that finds your games, works out what each one needs, and sets it up. One click per game.
docs.quick_start.way_manual_desc: Download the mod loader and the mod yourself, and unzip them into the game. Three steps, once per game.
docs.quick_start.both_ways: Both end with the same files in the same folder, and both lead to the same first launch.
docs.install_manual.title: Installing by hand
docs.install_manual.when_title: When this is the right way
docs.install_manual.when: When you want to see exactly what goes where, when a game sits somewhere unusual, or when the Manager refuses a game you know is fine. Nothing here is out of date — it is simply longer than the other way.
docs.first_launch.skip_wizard_title: You can answer this once, for every game
docs.first_launch.skip_wizard: The Manager holds the same questions under Mod defaults. Answer them there and games you set up afterwards start configured, without this wizard appearing at all.
docs.manager.title: The Manager
docs.manager.intro: UnityGameTranslator Manager is a desktop program for Windows and Linux. It sets your games up so the mod can do its work, and it keeps track of every game you have set up.
docs.manager.does_find: finds the Unity games on this machine — Steam, Epic and GOG on their own, anywhere else you point it
docs.manager.does_read: reads what each game is built with, and names the ones nothing can be installed into, and why
docs.manager.does_install: installs the mod loader a game needs, and the mod itself, and keeps both up to date
docs.manager.does_answer_once: answers the mod's first-run questions once, for every game, instead of once per game
docs.manager.does_oneclick: sets a game up in one click — loader, mod, settings and a community translation
docs.manager.does_ai: finds an AI server on this machine, and installs one if there is none
docs.manager.does_test: tries an AI model on the exact job the mod gives it, in the languages you play in
docs.manager.does_translations: brings down a translation the community published, and tells you when a newer one is out
docs.manager.does_standing: shows where each of your translations stands, and publishes, merges or edits it
docs.manager.does_backup: keeps a copy of a translation before anything replaces it
docs.manager.does_repair: recognises a game you set up by hand, and moves the mod to where its mod loader looks for it
docs.manager.does_other_account: leaves alone a game somebody else on this computer set up
docs.manager.does_remove: removes what it installed, file by file, and leaves everything else alone
docs.manager.not_a_translator: It never translates anything itself, and it does not run while you play. The mod does that, inside the game.
docs.manager.get_portable: Download it and run it. It works straight away from the file you downloaded — nothing is installed, and nothing is written outside its own folder.
docs.manager.get_install: The first time it opens, it offers to install itself on this machine. That puts it in your start menu with a proper way to remove it, and lets it update itself. It changes nothing in your games either way, and you can keep running it from the downloaded file for as long as you like.
docs.manager.shot_firstrun_alt: A banner at the top of the Manager offering to install the program on this machine.
docs.manager.shot_firstrun_caption: First launch. You can ignore the banner; it goes away once you answer it.
docs.manager.games_found: When it opens, the Manager shows every Unity game it found on this machine, and what each one needs. Steam, Epic and GOG libraries are found on their own.
docs.manager.shot_home_alt: The Manager's main window: the list of games found on this machine on the left, and on the right how many can take the mod, how many already have it, and how many have a translation waiting.
docs.manager.shot_home_caption: What the machine holds, before anything is touched.
docs.manager.games_play_in: Above the list, Play in is the language you want to play in. It decides what the whole window shows: which of your games are already playable, which have a translation waiting, and which have none yet.
docs.manager.games_tags: The tags narrow the list down: games already set up, games with a translation in your language, games nobody has translated yet, games you take part in, and the ones nothing can be installed into.
docs.manager.games_folders: For a game that is not in a Steam, Epic or GOG library — installed by hand, on a second drive, in a library you keep somewhere of your own — open My folders and add the folder. Each one is searched two levels deep.
docs.manager.shot_folders_alt: The folders window, listing two added folders, each saying how many games in the list came from it.
docs.manager.shot_folders_caption: Steam, Epic and GOG do not have to be added here. This is for everything else.
docs.manager.games_reads: For each game it reads what matters before anything is installed: the Unity version, whether the game is Mono or IL2CPP, whether it is 32-bit or 64-bit, and which mod loader fits. Without it, that is the check you would have to make yourself —
docs.manager.games_reads_link: see how it is done by hand
docs.manager.shot_detection_alt: What the Manager read from a game: type, Unity version, mod loader and mod version, followed by a line saying what setting it up would do.
docs.manager.shot_detection_caption: Read from the game's own files, not guessed — and the last line says what would happen.
docs.manager.refused_title: Games nothing can be installed into
docs.manager.refused_intro: A few games cannot take a mod at all — and that is not about this mod. Every mod for a Unity game runs inside a mod loader, and on these games no loader can start, so no mod of any kind can either. The Manager checks before offering anything, and says which games and why.
docs.manager.refused_store_why: The folder is locked down and the binaries are encrypted.
docs.manager.refused_stripped_why: The game was built with parts of its runtime library removed, and every mod loader needs them. BepInEx 5, BepInEx 6 and MelonLoader were each tried on such a game, and so was putting the missing libraries back.
docs.manager.refused_unreadable_why: Mono or IL2CPP, 32-bit or 64-bit — when a game does not say, installing the wrong one either stops it from starting or silently never runs.
docs.manager.refused_overrule: You can overrule any of these and try anyway. Everything the Manager installs is written down and can be removed, so a loader that turns out not to work costs you a few minutes and nothing else. A refused game also stays in your list — you play it from wherever you always did, the Manager simply offers nothing for it.
docs.manager.shot_refused_alt: A refused game: in the list, a red line saying it cannot be modded; in the card, a red-bordered box explaining why no mod loader can start on it.
docs.manager.shot_refused_caption: A refusal always says why, and says plainly that it is not a limitation of the tool.
docs.manager.refused_anticheat_title: A game with an anti-cheat, and this one cannot be overruled
docs.manager.refused_anticheat: Installing a mod loader into a game protected by EasyAntiCheat or BattlEye can get your account banned. The cost is yours, and no uninstall undoes it.
docs.manager.defaults_intro: The mod asks a few things the first time it runs in a game. Answer them once in Mod defaults, and every game you set up afterwards starts already configured. What it holds:
docs.manager.defaults_language: The language you play in. Everything else follows from it.
docs.manager.defaults_backend: How lines get translated. A game somebody has already translated needs none of this; the rest is for what nobody has translated yet.
docs.manager.defaults_ai: The AI server and the model, when that is the way you chose.
docs.manager.defaults_hotkey: The key that opens the mod inside a game.
docs.manager.defaults_online: Whether the mod may go online while you play, and whether it tells you about new versions.
docs.manager.shot_defaults_alt: The Mod defaults window: the language to play in, how lines get translated, the AI server and model, the key that opens the mod in a game, and what it may do online.
docs.manager.shot_defaults_caption: Filled in once. Every game set up afterwards starts with these settings.
docs.manager.defaults_first_title: This is what setting up in one click needs
docs.manager.defaults_first: Until Mod defaults has been filled in once, the Manager has nothing to configure a game with, and it says so rather than guessing: setting a game up would leave it running in its own language. Go through it once and every game becomes a single click. A game you have already configured is not touched until you ask.
docs.manager.defaults_ways: Each game says where its settings come from: the same answers as your other games, its own answers chosen on its card, or neither of the two — you let the mod's own setup wizard ask you inside the game, the one described under
docs.manager.shot_ways_alt: The three ways a game can be configured: use the shared defaults, let the mod ask inside the game, or choose the settings on this card.
docs.manager.shot_ways_caption: The middle one is offered only until the mod's wizard has run once in that game.
docs.manager.defaults_inherited: Choose the third and every field tells you where its value came from, so you change what you want to change and leave the rest. What each setting actually does is written under
docs.manager.shot_inherited_alt: A game's own settings: language, how lines get translated, AI server and model, each marked as coming from the shared defaults until it is changed.
docs.manager.shot_inherited_caption: Every field says where its value comes from.
docs.manager.defaults_key_title: The in-game key is the one setting a game does not inherit
docs.manager.defaults_key: The same key is not detected the same way in every game, and a game may already use it for something else. A game that already has one keeps it, and its card offers to replace it.
docs.manager.oneclick_intro: Pick a game and a bar appears at the bottom of the window. It lists what one click would do here, before you click, and the button is named after it. Depending on the game, it will:
docs.manager.oneclick_step_loader: install the mod loader, or update the one already there
docs.manager.oneclick_step_mod: install the mod, or update it
docs.manager.oneclick_step_settings: write your settings into the game, with the number of things that change
docs.manager.oneclick_step_translation: bring down a translation, if you left that box ticked
docs.manager.oneclick_nothing_else: Nothing else. It never removes anything, and it never publishes anything.
docs.manager.shot_oneclick_alt: A game not set up yet. The bar at the bottom lists what one click would do — install the mod loader, install the mod, apply the shared settings, take a community translation — beside a ticked box and the button that runs them.
docs.manager.shot_oneclick_caption: The bar always lists what one click would do, before you click.
docs.manager.oneclick_off_title: When the button is off, it says why
docs.manager.oneclick_off_intro: There are only a few reasons, and each one has a way out.
docs.manager.oneclick_off_done: Everything is in place and up to date. The button beside it starts the game.
docs.manager.oneclick_off_defaults: Nothing has been decided about what goes into your games yet. Open Mod defaults once and the button lights up for every game.
docs.manager.oneclick_off_notranslator: Nobody has published a translation for this game in your language, and no way of translating has been chosen. Pick one in Mod defaults — including writing the lines yourself — and the button comes back.
docs.manager.oneclick_off_running: Close the game: its files are locked while it runs.
docs.manager.oneclick_off_noloader: Nothing can be installed here. The card says what the game is built with.
docs.manager.oneclick_off_prereq_says: A missing prerequisite, named on the card
docs.manager.oneclick_off_prereq: Something the loader needs is not on this machine — the .NET Desktop Runtime, for instance.
docs.manager.oneclick_other_account_titl: A game somebody else set up
docs.manager.oneclick_other_account: One computer carries games belonging to different people. On a game whose mod is signed in as another account, the Manager will still install and update the mod — but it will not write settings and will not replace the translation. Undoing somebody else's work by accident is the one thing it refuses.
docs.manager.ai_intro: If nobody has translated your game yet, the mod can do it as you play: free, on your own machine, if it can run a model — or with a paid service and your own key. The settings are the same ones described under
docs.manager.ai_install_server: If nothing on this machine can translate, the Manager offers to install an AI server. It installs Ollama the usual way: the publisher's own installer, checked against the publisher's own checksum, with no administrator rights needed. On Linux it gives you the command instead of running it.
docs.manager.ai_hardware_title: This is where your machine matters
docs.manager.ai_hardware: A model runs on your graphics card — or failing that on your processor and memory — at the same time as the game. The smallest ones are well under what people expect, and the list below says what each one held when we ran it. But whether it fits and whether it is comfortable while a game is running are two different questions, and only your machine answers the second.
docs.manager.ai_any_server: The Manager looks for a server on this machine — it knows where Ollama and LM Studio usually sit — but it asks the same question the mod asks, so anything OpenAI-compatible answers: a server on another computer, one we have never heard of, or a paid service with your own key. The models already on your server fill the picker, whichever server it is.
docs.manager.ai_our_models: Models we have run ourselves is a different list, and a shorter one: the ones we measured, with what matters before downloading anything — how much video memory each held, how big the download is, how long a line took, and how much of the mod's own instruction set it followed. Your own card's memory is stated beside them, so the comparison is with your machine and not with ours.
docs.manager.shot_models_alt: The list of models the project has run, each with the video memory it held, its download size, the time it took per line, and how many instructions it followed.
docs.manager.shot_models_caption: Measured, not claimed — and compared against the card in your own machine.
docs.manager.ai_ollama_names: These are Ollama model names, and fetching one in a click is something only Ollama does. The figures hold on any server: install the model the way yours installs models, and it appears in the picker.
docs.manager.ai_test_title: Try a model before you rely on it
docs.manager.test_standalone_title: This test is worth it on its own
docs.manager.test_standalone: You do not need the Manager to look after your games to use this. If you already run a local AI and installed the mod by hand, this is the quickest way to find out whether your model is any good at translating a game — the checks are the mod's own. For now it lives only in the Manager.
docs.manager.ai_test: Test this model runs the model through the instructions the mod actually sends — the same prompts, the same retries, the same rules about what an answer may and may not contain — translating into the language you play in, from the language your games are written in. Twenty-two cases, from a two-word menu label to a paragraph carrying line breaks, inserted names and colour markers all at once.
docs.manager.shot_test_alt: The result of a model test, case by case: what was asked, what the model answered, how long it took and how many requests it cost.
docs.manager.shot_test_caption: Every answer is shown — the hard cases are the ones worth reading.
docs.manager.ai_read_answers: It shows you every answer, and that is the point. The automatic checks can tell whether a marker survived or whether punctuation was invented; they cannot tell whether the translation is any good. A model once produced fluent French while believing it was writing Breton, and passed every structural check ever written. So read the answers.
docs.manager.ai_selfmark_title: The mark out of ten is the model grading itself
docs.manager.ai_selfmark: Treat it as a hint and nothing more. A model cannot mark a language it does not really have — the one writing French while believing it was Breton would have given itself a good mark — and small models bunch everything between six and eight. What means something is the difference between two models on the same cases, never a single number.
docs.manager.card_two_sides: A game's card has two sides. One is about the translation: which one it runs, whose it is, how much of it is human work, and what you can do with it. The other is about the software: which loader is installed, which version of the mod, and what the mod uses in this game.
docs.manager.shot_card_alt: A game's card: the translation it runs with its chips and quality bar, the community translations published for it, and the bar at the bottom saying the game is fully set up.
docs.manager.shot_card_caption: Nothing left to arrange on this one, so the bar offers the way to play instead.
docs.manager.card_chips: The chips say what the translation is: whether it is published, whether it leads its lineage or contributes to somebody else's, whether it is up to date, how far along its author says it is, and how many people have downloaded and rated it. The bar underneath is what it is made of — lines written by a person, lines a person checked, lines an AI produced. What each of those means is explained under
docs.manager.card_actions: From here you can open a translation in your browser to edit it, publish what you have written, settle a conflict between your copy and the published one, or take a different translation altogether. Before any replacement, a copy of the old translation is kept.
docs.manager.card_other_language: The community list is not limited to the language you play in. If nobody has translated a game into it, you can take one in another language you read — the game is pointed at that language, and nothing else changes.
docs.manager.card_setup_tab: The other side shows what the game is built with, which loader is installed and whether a newer one is out, which version of the mod is there, and the settings the mod uses in this game.
docs.manager.updates_intro: Three things can have a new version, and none of them updates behind your back:
docs.manager.updates_mod: the mod — offered per game, and one click applies it
docs.manager.updates_loader: the mod loader — offered the same way, unless it was installed by something other than the Manager, in which case it is reported and left alone until you allow it
docs.manager.updates_tool: the Manager itself — it checks when it starts, says what it found, and waits
docs.manager.shot_loader_alt: A line on a game's card saying a newer mod loader is out, and that the Manager did not install the current one, so updating it has to be allowed first.
docs.manager.shot_loader_caption: It never takes over a mod loader it did not install without being asked.
docs.manager.remove_intro: Uninstall removes the mod from a game, file by file, from the record written when it was installed. Nothing else in the game is touched, and files you changed since installing are left alone.
docs.manager.remove_options: Two more things are offered and neither is ticked by default: removing the mod loader as well, and removing your settings and translations. A copy of the translation is kept aside before it goes, and the copies themselves stay.
docs.manager.byhand_title: If you already installed by hand
docs.manager.byhand_intro: Nothing to undo. Open the Manager and the game is in the list, with what it found: the loader, the mod, and the translation if there is one. Two things it may offer:
docs.manager.byhand_misplaced: the mod is not where the loader reads it. Some loaders only look in one folder, and a copy one level away is never loaded, with nothing to say so. The Manager moves it, and takes your settings and your translation with it.
docs.manager.byhand_copies: there is more than one copy of the mod. It offers to remove the ones that are not being read.
docs.manager.byhand_loader: The mod loader itself it leaves alone. It says when a newer one is out, and installs it only if you allow it: a loader you put there may be running other mods, and replacing it is not its call.
docs.manager.settings_intro: These are about the program itself, not about your games: the account it uses on this site, whether it may reach the internet at all, a proxy if your network needs one, which build of the mod it installs, and whether it looks for its own updates.
docs.manager.settings_account: Signing in is only needed to publish or to contribute. Downloading a published translation needs no account. How the account is linked is described under
